fields.title: Zaslon: Fourteen Action Items After the Outage
fields.summary: The COO announced that we are fixing everything. Two quarters of work. The plan is due on Friday.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you bring on Friday?
fields.brief/role: You are the PM of the platform team.
fields.brief/company: Zaslon is a fictional company of 300 people that sells a patient booking system to medical clinics.
fields.brief/context: On Tuesday, a database migration locked a table for nine hours during business hours. Clinics couldn't book or receive patients, affecting 1,900 clinics. The post-mortem yielded fourteen action items, and the COO told the board that "we are fixing everything." The head of development estimates these fourteen items will take two quarters. You are presenting the plan on Friday.
fields.brief/objective: Assemble a plan that the team will actually follow through on.
fields.brief/constraints: Six engineers. About a quarter before deferred work returns. Two out of the fourteen items are already in progress.
fields.brief/task: Decide what will go into the plan and justify your choice.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: A list of fourteen items is not a plan
fields.learnTakeaway/body: After an outage, the temptation is to promise everything, which guarantees that nothing gets finished: the team gets distracted, and there is no one to follow up. A plan should be validated against the history of failures — what has already happened and what each item would have caught — and your own capacity. The rest is not discarded but presented as a list with the cost and risk of each item: this is an honest conversation, and it resolves the question of "why not everything."
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
09:12 — migration starts. It adds a column with a default value, which locks the bookings table on this database version.
09:14 — error spike, an automated alert goes to the on-call channel.
09:31 — on-call engineer responds. The alert went to a channel, not a phone call; the engineer was in a meeting.
09:48 — root cause identified.
10:05 — attempt to roll back the migration fails: the operation is irreversible halfway through.
11:20 — decision made to restore from backup.
14:40 — restoration started after a dispute over who makes this decision.
18:05 — service is back up.

The status page was updated manually, twice in nine hours.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
In engineer-weeks:
1. A second engineer reviews migrations — 0.5 (in progress)
2. A rule banning blocking migration patterns on this database version — 1
3. Migrations only during the maintenance window, not business hours — 0.5
4. Alert calls the person instead of writing to a channel — 0.5
5. Documented restoration procedure plus a drill — 3
6. Automated status page updates based on error rates — 2
7. Database splitting for bookings — 12
8. Backup region — 20
9. Rewriting the migration layer — 8
10. Incident commander role with decision-making authority — 0.5
11. Client message templates — 1
12. Moving the table to a new database version — 6
13. Quarterly load testing drills — 2
14. Post-mortems every two weeks with one action item — 0.5
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Migrations run about 40 times a quarter. Over two years:
— 3 migrations caused customer-facing degradation. All 3 were blocking patterns that the rule from item 2 would have caught.
— 0 incidents were caused by a region failure, which item 8 addresses.
— 4 incidents over two years lasted more than an hour. In all four, the largest chunk of time was spent on decision-making, not the actual work.

In this outage: 36 minutes from error to root cause, 3 hours 15 minutes from root cause to restoration decision, 3 hours 25 minutes for the restoration itself.

Support handled 640 tickets; 70% asked what was happening and when it would be fixed.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
COO at the board meeting: "We are fixing all fourteen." In a conversation with you: "I need to tell the board that this won't happen again, and give the six clinics asking for guarantees something clear."

Head of development: "If I sign up for all fourteen, I'll do nine poorly, and the quarter will be wasted on context switching. I'd rather take six and finish them."

Head of support: "Give me a status page that updates automatically, and templates. I'll cut half the calls with just that."

In the previous post-mortem six months ago, there were nine items; only two were completed, and no one tracked the rest.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Prevention, response, and communication — with owners and deadlines
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Take items 1–6, 10, 11, and 14 — about 14 engineer-weeks — finish them, and present the remaining five as a list with dates, costs, and risks for each.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The choice is backed by history: all three major outages over two years were blocking migrations that the rule from item 2 would have caught, and the longest part of the four lengthy incidents was decision-making, which means items 10 and 5.
The team actually finishes nine items in 14 engineer-weeks over the quarter, each with an owner and a deadline.
Support gets the status page and templates — they estimate this cuts half of the 640 tickets.
Item 14 — post-mortems every two weeks with one action item — turns past history (nine items, two done, no one tracking) into a self-checking process.
You give the COO what he needs: "blocking migrations no longer pass automatically" — a verifiable statement for the board and the six clinics.
Trade-off: five items are left undone, and the phrase "fixing everything" had to be publicly clarified.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Take items 4, 5, 6, 10, and 11 — on-call phone alert, restoration procedure, status page, incident commander, templates — on the grounds that the nine hours were a failure of response, not migration.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The observation is correct: three and a quarter hours passed from root cause to decision, and in all four long incidents over two years, decision-making took longer than the work itself.
The team easily closes seven engineer-weeks, and the next incident indeed lasts two hours instead of nine.
But it still happens: the rule catching blocking migrations cost one week and was not taken, while migrations run 40 times a quarter.
The COO asks why the same thing happened again, and there is no answer to this question.
Trade-off: the duration of outages is fixed, but their cause is left untouched, even though prevention here was cheaper than response.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Take items 7, 8, 9, and 12 — database splitting, backup region, rewriting the migration layer, moving the table: process patches won't save you from the next, different failure.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
46 engineer-weeks against a quarter for six people is two quarters, and the work is finished neither by Friday nor by the end of the quarter.
The backup region costs 20 weeks and addresses a class of failures of which there has been none in two years.
During this time, migrations continue to run 40 times a quarter without the rule that would have cost one week.
Support continues to respond manually.
By the end of the quarter, only one and a half out of four items are done, leaving nothing to show the board.
Trade-off: the most fundamental solution was chosen instead of the one that directly addresses the known cause.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: The COO has already announced this to the board. Take a quarter and most of the next.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The list is accepted without argument, which is the only easy moment.
A quarter later, nine out of fourteen items are closed, four of them only halfway: the team spent the entire quarter context switching, exactly as the head of development warned.
The biweekly post-mortem, which cost half a week and would have kept the rest on track, ended up at the bottom of the list and was not done.
The six clinics asking for guarantees receive the answer "we are working on everything" — which means nothing.
Six months later, history repeats itself: out of nine items, only two were completed, as there was no one to track them.
Trade-off: the promise to the board was kept in words at the cost of getting nothing finished.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: No measurement of where work is stuck: waiting is not separated from active work
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Process discussions do not end with an action item that has an owner and a deadline
